items.stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
items.context_html: Every morning, the <u>batch of croissants rise</u> unevenly if the layered butter softens before the trays reach the oven.
items.why_correct_md: The subject is the singular **batch**, so it needs a singular verb; the prepositional phrase 'of croissants' cannot control agreement.
items.why_tempted_md: The plural noun sitting directly beside the verb makes a plural verb sound natural to the ear.
items.rule_md: 1) Find the verb. 2) Ask 'who or what does this?' 3) Cross out any prepositional phrase ('of ___') between subject and verb. 4) Match the verb to the head noun that remains. 5) Reread the sentence to confirm it sounds right without the crossed-out phrase.

per_choice_rationale.A: Nearest-noun trap: the verb has been matched to the plural 'croissants' inside the prepositional phrase instead of to the singular subject 'batch.'
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the true subject is the singular 'batch,' so it takes the singular verb; 'of croissants' is only a modifier.
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a plural verb and needlessly shifts into a progressive form, both of which fail with the singular, habitual subject.
per_choice_rationale.D: Rewrites the subject instead of fixing the verb — and the new plural 'batches' still disagrees with the singular verb.

hints.body_md: Think about who or what is doing the rising here.
Try crossing out any 'of ___' phrase between the subject and its verb, then test the agreement again.
Which single noun is the true subject — the container, or the pastries tucked inside the phrase?
The head of this subject is the singular 'batch'; 'of croissants' is a modifier that cannot control the verb. Make the verb agree with 'batch' and choose again.
What made this one stand out to you?
Two things shifted in this version — check the verb's number and its tense against the original sentence.
Is the subject 'batch' singular or plural, and did the sentence need to move into an ongoing '-ing' form?
This version uses a plural verb and shifts the tense; the subject 'batch' is singular and the sentence describes a habitual event, so keep a simple singular present verb and re-choose.
Say more about what this version fixes.
Watch out for options that rewrite the subject itself — check whether the new subject and verb even agree with each other.
If the subject became the plural 'batches,' what verb form would it then require?
This option shuffles the nouns yet still pairs a plural subject with a singular verb; the cleanest fix keeps the original singular subject and adjusts only the verb. Choose again.

items.stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
items.context_html: The saucier <u>who the head chef trusted</u> with the evening's consommé had apprenticed for a decade in Marseille.

choices.label: whom the head chef trusted him

items.why_correct_md: The pronoun is the **object** of 'trusted' — the head chef trusted *her* — so the object-case relative pronoun is required.
items.why_tempted_md: Because the pronoun appears right where a subject usually sits, before 'the head chef,' the subject form sounds natural.
items.rule_md: 1) Isolate the relative clause. 2) Rearrange it into a plain sentence: 'the head chef trusted ___.' 3) Test with he/him: if *him* fits, use the object-case relative pronoun; if *he* fits, use the subject form. 4) Confirm the pronoun refers to a person, not a thing. 5) Check that no extra pronoun repeats the same slot.

per_choice_rationale.A: Case error: the pronoun is the object of 'trusted' (the head chef trusted *her*), so the subject form fails.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the relative pronoun receives the action of 'trusted,' so it must take the object case.
per_choice_rationale.C: Uses a relative pronoun reserved for things to refer to a person.
per_choice_rationale.D: Pronoun doubling: the relative pronoun already fills the object slot, so adding 'him' names the object twice.

hints.body_md: If you covered up the pronoun, who is doing the trusting in that clause?
Run the substitution test: turn the clause into a plain sentence using 'he' or 'him' and see which one fits.
The head chef trusted ___ — would you fill that slot with a subject pronoun or an object pronoun?
Because the pronoun receives the action of 'trusted,' it must take the object case; the subject form written here is the classic trap. Re-choose with the him-test in mind.
How would you describe the person this clause points back to?
Recall which relative pronouns English reserves for people and which for things.
Would you refer to a trained saucier the way you would refer to a saucepan?
This relative pronoun can only stand in for things; a person requires a personal relative pronoun in the case the clause demands — here, the object of 'trusted.' Choose again.
Read the clause aloud — where does your ear stumble?
Count how many words are receiving the action of 'trusted' in this version.
If the relative pronoun already serves as the object of 'trusted,' what is 'him' doing there?
This version names the object twice — the relative pronoun and 'him' fill the same slot. Keep the object-case pronoun and drop the duplicate, then re-choose.

items.stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?
items.context_html: In early New Orleans funeral processions, brass bands played solemn hymns on the march to the cemetery and raucous stomps on <u>they're return</u> to town.
items.why_correct_md: The slot needs the **possessive** form to show whose return it is.
items.why_tempted_md: *They're* sounds identical to the possessive when read aloud, so ear-spellers accept it without testing the expansion.
items.rule_md: 1) Expand the word: does *they are* make sense in the slot? 2) If yes, the apostrophe form is right; if no, reject it. 3) If the word answers *whose?*, use the possessive spelling. 4) If it answers *where?*, use the t-h-e-r-e spelling. 5) Reread the sentence with your pick.

per_choice_rationale.A: confused_homophone: *they're* is the contraction of *they are*, which cannot show possession of *return*.
per_choice_rationale.B: *There* points to a place and never marks possession, so it cannot tell whose return this is.
per_choice_rationale.C: Expanding the contraction to *they are return* produces nonsense, proving a subject-verb pair cannot fill this slot.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: the possessive *their* shows that the return belongs to the bands.

hints.body_md: Walk me through how you tested the underlined word before keeping it.
This word is a contraction — try replacing any contraction with its full two-word form and rereading the sentence.
Does 'raucous stomps on they are return to town' make sense once you expand it?
A contraction only works where its expanded form works; since the expansion fails here, the sentence needs the form that shows the return belongs to the bands — go back and find it.
What question is this word answering in the sentence — whose, or where?
One of these sound-alike spellings points to a place; check whether the sentence is naming a location or an owner.
Can a word that means 'in that place' describe whose return this is?
The t-h-e-r-e spelling only marks location; the sentence needs a possessive that ties the return to the bands, so choose the spelling that shows ownership.
Read the sentence aloud with your substitution in place — what do you hear?
Test whether a subject-plus-verb pair can sit in front of a noun like 'return' this way.
Would you say 'on we are return' or 'on our return'? Which pattern does this slot demand?
A pronoun-verb pair cannot modify the noun that follows; the slot calls for a single possessive word showing whose return it is, so re-choose with that in mind.

items.stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
items.context_html: At its annual fan appreciation night, the Meadowlark Falls Owls handed out <u>not only free caps and</u> vouchers for discounted season tickets.

choices.label: not only free caps as well as
not only free caps, and also
not only free caps but also

items.why_correct_md: **Correlative** conjunctions come in fixed pairs, and this choice completes the pair that 'not only' opens.
items.why_tempted_md: 'As well as' sounds natural in everyday speech, so students accept it as an interchangeable substitute for the fixed pair.
items.rule_md: 1) Spot a pair-opener such as 'not only,' 'either,' 'neither,' or 'both.' 2) Recall the one fixed partner that opener requires. 3) Scan ahead in the sentence for that exact partner. 4) If any other connector sits in its place, replace it with the fixed partner. 5) Confirm the two joined elements are parallel in form.

per_choice_rationale.A: Leaves 'not only' hanging without its required partner conjunction; a plain 'and' cannot complete the correlative pair.
per_choice_rationale.B: Substitutes the near-synonym 'as well as' for the fixed partner that 'not only' demands (correlative_wrong_partner).
per_choice_rationale.C: Adds a comma and 'also,' but the correlative pair is still broken because the fixed partner phrase never appears.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'not only' must be completed by its fixed correlative partner, which this choice supplies.

hints.body_md: Walk me through how the two giveaway items in this sentence are linked together.
Certain opening phrases in English lock a sentence into a matching phrase later on — check whether this sentence opens one of those pairs.
The phrase 'not only' makes a promise about what comes next; does a plain 'and' deliver on that promise?
'Not only' is a correlative opener that must be completed by its one fixed partner phrase, so leaving 'and' in place breaks the pair — look for the option that supplies the partner.
What made 'as well as' feel like the right connector here?
Test whether this connector is the officially matched partner for the phrase that opens the pair, not just a phrase with a similar meaning.
'As well as' can join items in many sentences — but is it the one partner that grammar assigns to 'not only'?
Correlative pairs are fixed, not interchangeable with synonyms; 'as well as' expresses addition but is not the sanctioned partner of 'not only,' so re-choose with the fixed pair in mind.
Say more about what the comma plus connector is doing for this sentence.
When a sentence opens a paired conjunction, check the exact wording — and the punctuation — that the pair requires.
Does inserting a comma before the connector fix the mismatch, or does 'not only' still lack its true partner?
A comma cannot rescue a broken correlative pair; 'not only' still needs its fixed partner phrase rather than ', and also,' so revisit the options for the standard pairing.

items.stem_md: Which choice conforms to the conventions of standard written English?
items.context_html: County health codes <u>prohibit vendors to sell</u> samples that have sat unrefrigerated for more than two hours.
items.why_correct_md: The verb **prohibit** takes the fixed pattern 'prohibit someone from doing something.'
items.why_tempted_md: 'Forbid vendors to sell' is standard English, so students transfer the infinitive pattern onto 'prohibit.'
items.rule_md: 1) Identify the verb that controls the underlined pattern. 2) Recall its fixed companion pattern by testing a familiar example ('the sign prohibits visitors ___ feeding the ducks'). 3) Eliminate any option that borrows a different verb's pattern. 4) Eliminate any option missing the required connector. 5) Confirm the survivor reads naturally in the sentence.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Prohibit' does not take a to-infinitive; this borrows the pattern of 'forbid' (idiom_wrong_pattern).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct — 'prohibit' idiomatically takes an object plus 'from' with an -ing form.
per_choice_rationale.C: Hypercorrects with a 'that' clause, a structure 'prohibit' does not allow (idiom_that_clause).
per_choice_rationale.D: Drops the required preposition, leaving a nonstandard shortcut (idiom_dropped_prep).

hints.body_md: Before checking anything else, say the underlined phrase out loud — does it sound like standard usage to you?
Think about which small connecting words the verb 'prohibit' normally travels with.
You can 'forbid someone to do' something — but does 'prohibit' follow that same pattern, or does it demand a different connector?

English verbs carry fixed companion patterns, and 'prohibit' rejects the to-infinitive used here; recall how you'd finish 'The sign prohibits visitors ___ feeding the ducks,' then re-choose accordingly.
Say more about why a 'that' clause seemed like the right fix here.
Consider whether 'prohibit' can hand its action off to a full clause the way 'require' or 'insist' can.
Would you ever write 'The rule prohibits that we park here' in careful prose?

'Prohibit' takes a person or thing as its object plus a fixed connector pattern, not a 'that' clause; since this version borrows the wrong verb's structure, test each option in a simple sentence and re-choose.
Tell me what connects 'vendors' to 'selling' in this version.
Check whether the verb's required linking word survived in this shortened phrasing.
If a sign 'prohibits visitors feeding the ducks,' is anything missing between the person and the action?
Dropping the small connector that 'prohibit' requires leaves a nonstandard shortcut; restore the verb's full companion pattern in your head, then re-evaluate the options.

items.stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
items.context_html: Audiences in 1914 gasped as Gertie the Dinosaur lumbered across the screen; Winsor McCay <u>stands</u> beside the projection each night and pretended to command his hand-drawn creature.
items.why_correct_md: Simple past **matches the time frame** established by 'gasped' and 'pretended.'
items.why_tempted_md: 'Had stood' sounds appropriately 'past,' so students reach for it even though no second, later past event requires past perfect.
items.rule_md: 1) List every verb in the sentence and its tense. 2) Identify the controlling time frame from dates and the other verbs. 3) Make the underlined verb match that frame. 4) Use past perfect only if the action must be shown finished before another past action.

per_choice_rationale.A: The present-tense 'stands' clashes with the past-tense narrative ('gasped,' 'pretended') and the 1914 setting.
per_choice_rationale.B: The simple past 'stood' matches 'gasped' and 'pretended,' keeping the sentence in one consistent past time frame.
per_choice_rationale.C: Past perfect 'had stood' wrongly signals the standing was completed before another past event, but no such later reference event exists.
per_choice_rationale.D: The present progressive 'is standing' places the action in the present moment, contradicting the past-tense verbs around it.

hints.body_md: Walk me through the moment this sentence describes — when is it happening?
Scan every verb in the sentence and note the time period each one signals; a sentence usually keeps its verbs anchored to one time.
The sentence says McCay 'pretended' to command the creature — does the underlined verb match the time of 'pretended'?

Verbs in one sentence must stay in a consistent time frame unless the meaning truly shifts; a present-tense verb clashes with the past-tense 'pretended' and the 1914 setting, so revisit the tenses on offer.
What made you reach for a two-word verb form here?
Think about what the 'had + verb' construction signals; it is used to order two past events, not just to sound more past.
Is there a second, later past event in this sentence that his standing must be placed before?

Past perfect marks an action completed before another past action; nothing in this sentence happens after the standing in a way that requires that earlier layer, so a simpler past-time form is all the sentence needs — decide again with that in mind.
Read the sentence aloud — what year does it keep pointing back to?
Check the helping verb: what time does it place the action in, and does that match the rest of the sentence?
Can an ongoing present-time action sit comfortably beside 'gasped' and 'pretended'?
An 'is + -ing' form describes something happening right now, but every other verb and the 1914 date set this scene firmly in the past, so the tense must match that earlier time — reconsider.

items.stem_md: Which choice best fits the sequence of events in the sentence?
items.context_html: By the time the researchers reached the shore at dawn, the highest pools <u>already dried</u> under the summer sun.
items.why_correct_md: An action completed **before** another past action takes the past perfect ('had' + past participle).
items.why_tempted_md: Both events are in the past, so students use simple past for both and miss the earlier-than relationship.
items.rule_md: 1) Identify the two past events. 2) Decide which happened first. 3) Put the earlier one in past perfect ('had' + participle). 4) Keep the later one in simple past.

per_choice_rationale.A: Simple past does not show that the drying finished before the past arrival, so a past perfect is required (tense_sequence).
per_choice_rationale.B: This drops the verb entirely, turning the clause into an ungrammatical fragment.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the past perfect shows the drying was completed before the past-tense arrival.
per_choice_rationale.D: Present perfect clashes with the clearly past verb 'reached.'

hints.body_md: What would change if you asked which event finished first, the arrival or the drying?
Look at whether two past actions happen at the same moment or one clearly precedes the other.
When one past event is completed before a second past event, should both verbs sit in the same simple tense?
Two past actions in sequence need the earlier one marked as finished-before; a plain simple-past verb flattens that order, so the timing is lost here.
Read the clause aloud — does it still contain a working verb describing the pools?
Check that the underlined words actually include an action, not just a description.
Without a verb of action, can the clause tell the reader that something happened to the pools?
This version leaves a describing word where a verb belongs, so the clause has no action and cannot express the completed event; it is not grammatical.
Say more about how the helper verb you chose connects to a scene that already happened at dawn.
Match the tense of the underlined verb to the clearly past verb in the main clause.
Does a tense that links past to present fit a sentence anchored entirely in one past morning?
Present perfect ties an action to now, but this sentence is fixed in the past; the helper verb clashes with the past-tense arrival, so the sequence breaks.

items.stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?
items.context_html: Each of the twelve solar-powered stations along the ridge transmits <u>their</u> readings to the observatory every ten seconds.
items.why_correct_md: **Each** is grammatically singular, so the possessive pronoun referring to it must be singular.
items.why_tempted_md: The plural noun *stations* sits right beside the pronoun's slot, luring students into matching the nearest noun instead of the true antecedent *each*.
items.rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun and ask what it stands for. 2) Trace back to the true antecedent — with 'each of the X,' the antecedent is *each*, not X. 3) Decide singular or plural from that antecedent. 4) Separately test any apostrophe by expanding it ('it is' / 'they are') and re-reading the sentence.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their' is plural, but the true antecedent 'each' is singular, so the pronoun disagrees in number.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'It's' is the contraction of 'it is,' not a possessive, so it cannot show ownership of the readings.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: a singular possessive pronoun matches the singular antecedent 'each.'
per_choice_rationale.D: 'They're' means 'they are' — a plural contraction, not a possessive of any kind.

hints.body_md: What word in the sentence is this pronoun standing in for — say it out loud.
Watch out for the noun that sits closest to the blank; the real antecedent may be further back, at the head of the subject.
Is the subject 'each' or 'stations'? Strip away 'of the twelve solar-powered stations' and see what's left to own the readings.
'Each' is grammatically singular even when a plural noun follows it in an of-phrase, so a plural possessive can't refer back to it. Rework the number match and pick again.
If you covered up the apostrophe for a second, what is this word actually built from?
Run the expansion test on any apostrophe-plus-s pronoun: swap in the two words it abbreviates and re-read.
Does 'transmits it is readings' make sense? What does that tell you about putting a contraction in a possessive slot?
An apostrophe in this pronoun always signals the contraction 'it is,' never possession — the possessive form carries no apostrophe. With that rule in hand, reconsider the choices.
Say more about what this word expands to when you write it out fully.
Two separate checks apply here: number (singular or plural?) and form (possessive or contraction?). Run both.
The subject is 'each' — singular — and the sentence needs a word showing ownership of the readings. Does a plural contraction pass either test?
This word fails twice: it abbreviates 'they are,' so it isn't possessive, and it's plural while the antecedent 'each' is singular. Apply both tests and choose again.

items.stem_md: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
items.context_html: By the time the 1900 hurricane reached the Texas coast, forecasters at the national office <u>have dismissed</u> the warnings that Cuban meteorologists had cabled days earlier.
items.why_correct_md: **Past perfect** places the dismissal before the landfall, the sentence's other past event.
items.why_tempted_md: 'Were dismissing' sounds convincingly past, so students accept it without checking whether the action was already finished before landfall.
items.rule_md: 1) Find the time anchor ('By the time X happened...'). 2) Ask: was the underlined action finished before that anchor? 3) If yes, use past perfect (had + past participle). 4) If it was ongoing at the anchor, use past progressive; if simultaneous, simple past. 5) Re-read the sentence to confirm the sequence.

per_choice_rationale.A: Present perfect 'have dismissed' ties the action to the present moment, but the sentence is anchored to a past event in 1900 (misconception: present perfect for remote past).
per_choice_rationale.B: Future perfect 'will have dismissed' points to completion before a future moment, yet every event here is past (misconception: any perfect form fits 'by the time').
per_choice_rationale.C: Past progressive 'were dismissing' portrays the action as ongoing at landfall, but 'days earlier' shows it was already complete (misconception: progressive equals past-sounding vividness).
per_choice_rationale.D: Past perfect 'had dismissed' correctly marks an action completed before another past event, the landfall.

hints.body_md: Walk me through the timeline of this sentence — which event happened first, the cabled warnings or the landfall?
Check the tense frame: the sentence anchors everything to a moment in 1900, so test whether the underlined verb points to the present or to that past moment.
The helper verb in the original connects an action to right now. Can an action that ended before a 1900 landfall still be tied to the present?

Present perfect links a past action to the present moment, but this dismissal was completed before another past event; an earlier-than-past action needs a different perfect form. Revisit the options with that timeline in mind.
What made a future-pointing form feel right for events from 1900?
Run a timeline check: place the landfall and the dismissal on a line and ask which direction this tense points.
That form describes something that will be finished at a future moment. Is anything in this sentence still ahead of us?
Future perfect marks completion before a future deadline, yet both events here sit firmly in the past, so a forward-looking verb cannot fit. Re-test each option against the 1900 time frame.
Say more about why an in-progress form appealed to you here.
Try an aspect check: does the sentence describe an action still unfolding at landfall, or one already over and done?
The phrase 'days earlier' tells you when the dismissing happened. Was it still going on as the storm arrived?

Past progressive shows an action in motion at a past moment, but this action had wrapped up days before the landfall; a completed earlier action needs a perfect form instead. Look again with that distinction.

items.stem_md: Which choice is correct for the underlined portion?
items.context_html: Neither of the cider barns, which have stood beside the packing shed since the 1920s, has lost <u>their roofs</u> to a winter storm.
items.why_correct_md: **Neither** is grammatically singular, so the pronoun referring back to it must be singular.
items.why_tempted_md: The plural 'barns' sits close to the pronoun, luring students into plural agreement with the wrong word.
items.rule_md: 1) Find the pronoun's true antecedent, not the nearest noun. 2) Cross out interrupting phrases ('of the...', 'which...'). 3) Classify the antecedent as singular or plural (neither, either, each = singular). 4) Match the pronoun's number, then confirm it is a true possessive rather than a contraction.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Their roofs' treats the singular subject 'neither' as plural, matching the nearby plural 'barns' instead.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Their' still agrees with the nearest noun rather than with the singular pronoun 'neither.'
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They're' is the contraction of 'they are,' not a possessive, and the plural reference is wrong anyway.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: 'neither' is singular, so the singular possessive 'its' and singular 'roof' agree with it.

hints.body_md: What word do you think this pronoun is standing in for?
Try an agreement check: cross out every phrase between the subject and the pronoun before matching them.
When you strip away 'of the cider barns' and the clause after it, what single word is actually doing the losing?
Words like 'neither' and 'each' count as singular no matter what plural noun follows them, so a plural pronoun cannot refer back to one — pick again with that subject in mind.
Say more about why you kept the first word of the span but shrank the noun.
Check the pronoun against its true antecedent, not against the noun sitting closest to it.
Is 'neither' a plural word, and if not, can a plural pronoun point back to it?
'Neither' is singular, so both the possessive pronoun and the noun it governs must be singular; this version still carries a plural pronoun, so reconsider.
How did you decide between the two spellings that sound alike here?
Run a substitution test: expand any apostrophe-bearing pronoun into its full two-word form and reread.
Does 'they are roofs' make sense in this spot, and does a plural pronoun even match 'neither'?
An apostrophe in this pronoun signals the contraction 'they are,' never possession, and the antecedent 'neither' is singular besides — choose again.

items.stem_md: Which choice makes the meaning of the sentence clearest?
items.context_html: After the hitting coach reviews video with each young slugger, <u>the coach</u> records the agreed-upon swing adjustments in a shared notebook.
items.why_correct_md: With two candidates in the opening clause, only the **repeated noun** leaves zero doubt about who keeps the notebook.
items.why_tempted_md: Students trained to avoid repetition reach for 'he,' overlooking that two males in the sentence make the pronoun ambiguous.
items.rule_md: 1) Circle every person or thing named before the pronoun. 2) If more than one could grammatically be the referent, the pronoun is ambiguous. 3) Test each candidate in the pronoun's slot; if two readings both make sense, replace the pronoun with the specific noun. 4) Re-read to confirm one, and only one, meaning survives.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: with two possible people in the first clause, repeating the noun is the only way to make the recorder unmistakable.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'He' could refer to either the coach or the slugger, leaving the doer ambiguous (pronoun_two_referents).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'They' either invents a joint actor the sentence never establishes or leaves the recorder vague (vague_plural_pronoun).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'This' is a bare demonstrative with no noun to stand for, so the doer disappears entirely (demonstrative_no_antecedent).

hints.body_md: Picture the scene — two people are in that video room. Who do you see writing in the notebook?
Whenever a pronoun follows a clause containing more than one possible person, test each candidate in its place.
Could a reader defensibly claim the slugger, rather than the instructor, is doing the recording in your version?
A pronoun with two plausible antecedents creates ambiguity, and this one could name either person in the sentence; clarity requires an unmistakable reference, so re-choose.
How many people would 'they' refer to in your reading of the sentence?
Check plural pronouns against the sentence: is there a plural noun — or a clearly established pair — meant to act here?
If both people together kept the notebook, would the sentence's point about who tracks the adjustments survive?
'They' either invents a joint actor the sentence never sets up or leaves the doer vague; the sentence needs one clearly identified recorder, so revise your selection.
If you covered up the rest of the sentence, what would 'this' point to?
Demonstratives need a concrete noun to lean on — hunt for the noun that 'this' would stand in for.
Does 'this' name a person at all, or does it leave the keeper of the notebook unidentified?
A bare demonstrative cannot clearly stand for a person previously named, so the doer of the recording vanishes; choose the version that leaves no doubt about who writes the notes.

items.stem_md: The writer wants an opening sentence that introduces the paragraph's focus on how deep-sea creatures produce their own glow. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
items.context_html: _____ Certain anglerfish dangle a glowing lure to draw victims close, while some squid release clouds of luminous mucus to confuse predators. Even tiny dinoflagellates flash blue when the water around them is disturbed.

choices.label: The deep sea is the largest habitat on Earth.
In the sunless depths, many organisms create their own glow through chemical reactions.
Anglerfish are among the strangest fish in the entire ocean.
Sunlight cannot reach the deepest parts of the ocean.

items.why_correct_md: An effective opener previews the **specific idea** the supporting sentences develop — here, self-produced glow.
items.why_tempted_md: The single-creature sentence echoes the first example, so students mistake a narrow detail for a topic sentence.
items.rule_md: 1) Read the supporting sentences and state their shared idea. 2) An opener should preview that exact idea. 3) Reject sentences that are broader than the idea, narrower than it, or off its topic. 4) Confirm the opener sets up every example that follows.

per_choice_rationale.A: Makes a sweeping claim about ocean size that the examples never address, so it is too broad (intro_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it names the shared ability the following examples all illustrate, framing the paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.C: Spotlights only one of the several creatures listed, so it is too narrow to introduce them all (intro_too_narrow).
per_choice_rationale.D: Describes the dark setting but not the ability the examples demonstrate, so it fails to introduce the focus (intro_offtopic).

hints.body_md: Read the three sentences that follow — what single idea do they all illustrate?
An opener should preview the specific idea the examples develop; check whether this one reaches far wider than that.
Do the examples that follow discuss the size of the ocean, or a particular ability the creatures share?
This sentence makes a sweeping claim about ocean size, which the examples never touch; a strong opener should name the specific ability the following sentences illustrate — reconsider.
Count the creatures the following sentences describe — is it just one, or several?
An opening line should set up everything the paragraph discusses; check whether this one covers all the examples or just one.
The paragraph mentions several very different creatures — does zeroing in on a single one prepare the reader for the rest?
This spotlights just one of the several creatures listed, so it is too narrow to introduce a paragraph about all of them; the opener should frame the shared trait — try again.
What exactly do the examples show the creatures doing?
An effective opener should point at the behavior the examples demonstrate, not just the surroundings; check what this sentence actually announces.
Does this line describe what the creatures can do, or only how dark the place where they live is?
This sets the scene of a dark environment but never previews the ability the examples all demonstrate, so it does not truly introduce the paragraph's focus — reconsider.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main focus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: [The writer will add an introductory sentence here.] Hours before the gates open, he drags and waters the infield until the clay is uniform. Next he mows the outfield in alternating stripes and repaints the batter's boxes. Finally, he walks the foul lines with a string level, checking for the slightest crown. By the national anthem, every surface has met his exacting standard.

choices.label: Corliss Park hosts more than sixty home games every season.
Corliss Park's infield grass is a hybrid variety bred to survive humid summers.
Ray Delgado attended games at Corliss Park long before he worked there.
Each home date at Corliss Park begins with the same demanding checklist for groundskeeper Ray Delgado.

items.why_correct_md: An effective introduction must **preview** the paragraph's content, and only this choice names the worker and sets up his pregame tasks.
items.why_tempted_md: The biography option mentions the right person, so students accept it without checking whether it sets up what the paragraph actually does.
items.rule_md: 1) Read the body of the paragraph first and summarize its focus in five words. 2) Ask what a reader must know for sentence two to make sense. 3) Test each opener: does it name that focus and point forward to it? 4) Eliminate openers that are broader, narrower, or angled at a different subject. 5) Pick the one that forecasts the body.

per_choice_rationale.A: A schedule statistic never mentions the worker or his tasks, so it fails to preview the paragraph and leaves 'he' unexplained (intro_too_broad).
per_choice_rationale.B: A turf-botany detail points the paragraph toward grass science rather than the worker's pregame labor (intro_wrong_emphasis).
per_choice_rationale.C: Introduces the right person but frames his past as a fan, while the paragraph chronicles his present duties (intro_wrong_angle).
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the worker and previews the sequence of pregame tasks that every following sentence describes.

hints.body_md: What would a reader expect the paragraph to discuss after your opening line?
A strong opener should forecast the content that follows — inventory what the next sentences actually describe.
The body follows one worker's pregame tasks; does a stat about how many games the park hosts point a reader toward that?

An introduction must preview the paragraph's actual content, and a schedule statistic never mentions the worker whose tasks fill every following sentence — pick the opener that sets up his pregame labor.
How does turf science connect to what the rest of the paragraph describes?
Compare your opener's topic with the topic of the sentences that follow — do they share a focus?
The following sentences track a person moving through his morning tasks; does a fact about grass breeding introduce that person or those tasks?
This opener spotlights botany, but the paragraph is organized around one man's pregame duties, so the grass detail misdirects the reader — choose the sentence that frames his work.
What made the biographical detail feel like the right doorway into this paragraph?
Weigh whether your opener sets up what the paragraph does next or just shares background about the person.
The body describes what Delgado does on the morning of a game, not his history as a fan — which opener points to the doing?

Although this sentence introduces the right person, it frames his past as a spectator while the paragraph chronicles his present work, so it aims the reader at the wrong subject — select the opener about his duties.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to close the paragraph by emphasizing the saguaro's role as a home for many different kinds of creatures. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: The saguaro does far more than tower over the Sonoran Desert. Gila woodpeckers drill nest holes in its trunk, and when they abandon them, elf owls and purple martins take up residence. Insects tunnel through its pulp, and hawks perch on its crown to scan the flats for prey.

choices.label: A mature saguaro can keep growing for more than two centuries before it finally topples.
In this way a single saguaro becomes a crowded apartment tower, housing birds, insects, and mammals under one spiny roof.
The Gila woodpecker, in particular, could not raise its young without the cactus.
The saguaro also hoards enormous reserves of water inside its pleated trunk.

items.why_correct_md: The goal asks for a close that stresses **variety of inhabitants**, and only this option gathers birds, insects, and mammals together.
items.why_tempted_md: The water-storage line sounds impressively factual and stays on the saguaro, so students grab it even though it drops the habitat focus.
items.rule_md: 1) Restate the stated goal in a few words (here: shelters many kinds of creatures). 2) Read each option and ask whether it delivers that exact emphasis. 3) Cross out any option that changes the topic, narrows to one case, or shifts the emphasis. 4) Keep the one that captures the full breadth named in the goal. 5) Re-read it against the goal to confirm the match.

per_choice_rationale.A: Shifts to the plant's lifespan, ignoring the requested emphasis on the many creatures it shelters (add_offtopic).
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it sums up the paragraph by stressing the wide variety of animals the cactus shelters at once.
per_choice_rationale.C: Narrows to a single species, undercutting the goal of stressing many different creatures (goal_too_narrow).
per_choice_rationale.D: Redirects to water storage, an emphasis the goal does not ask for (goal_wrong_emphasis).

hints.body_md: Before checking the options, restate the goal in your own words — what should the closing line stress?
A closing sentence has to hit the specific emphasis the prompt names, not just mention the same subject.
Does a fact about how long the plant lives say anything about the range of animals that live on it?
The goal asks the ending to stress the many creatures the cactus shelters, but a lifespan fact abandons that focus; choose the line that gathers the variety of inhabitants instead.
What relationship do you see between a lone named bird and the goal's phrase 'many different kinds of creatures'?
Check whether the option covers the full breadth the goal names or zooms in on just a solitary case.
If the aim is to stress variety, does spotlighting a solitary species deliver that, or does it shrink the scope?
Focusing on a solitary species works against a goal about many kinds of animals; the closing should capture the whole range, so re-choose.
Which emphasis does the goal ask for, and does a line about stored water match it?
Test each option against the exact emphasis named in the prompt before judging how factual it sounds.
Is a detail about moisture reserves about the creatures the cactus houses, or about a different trait entirely?
The goal targets the cactus as a shelter for varied animals, so a water-storage detail shifts the emphasis; pick the option that stresses the many inhabitants.

items.stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?
items.context_html: Many beginners assume the amber safelight is completely harmless to photographic paper. <u>Similarly,</u> a sheet left under the lamp for several minutes will slowly fog.
items.why_correct_md: The second sentence **contradicts** the beginners' assumption, so the transition must signal contrast.
items.why_tempted_md: Both sentences mention the safelight and paper, so 'Similarly' feels superficially right to students who match topics instead of logic.
items.rule_md: 1) Restate each sentence in five plain words. 2) Name the relationship between them: same direction, contrast, cause-effect, or example. 3) Match the transition word to that named relationship. 4) Re-read the pair with your choice inserted to confirm the logic clicks.

per_choice_rationale.A: Treats the two sentences as alike (transition_false_similarity), but the second sentence contradicts the beginners' assumption rather than resembling it.
per_choice_rationale.B: Claims the fogging results from the assumption (transition_false_cause), though a belief cannot cause paper to fog.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: the second sentence reverses the expectation set up by the first, so a contrast word fits the logic.
per_choice_rationale.D: Presents the fogging as an illustration of the assumption (transition_false_example), when it actually disproves that assumption.

hints.body_md: What relationship do the two sentences actually have — does the second continue the first idea or push against it?
Restate each sentence in five plain words, then name the logic between them before judging any connector.
'Similarly' promises two alike ideas; is a belief that the light is harmless really alike to paper fogging under that light?

The first sentence reports what beginners assume, and the second reports the opposite reality, so the connector must signal contrast; a same-direction word points the wrong way, so re-name the logic and re-choose.
How did you decide that the second sentence is a result of the first?
Test cause and effect in both directions: does assuming the light is harmless actually cause the paper to fog?
If the belief in the first sentence were true, would the second sentence be expected — or surprising?
A result word claims the first sentence causes the second, but here the second sentence contradicts the assumption instead of following from it; the passage needs a contrast signal, so re-select.
Tell me what the second sentence would be an example of, if it were one.
An example must illustrate the claim before it; check whether the fogging paper supports or undercuts the beginners' assumption.
Can a statement that disproves a belief serve as an example of that same belief?
'For example' introduces support, yet this second sentence pushes back against the assumption before it; the logic calls for a contrast connector rather than an illustration, so choose again.

items.stem_md: Which transition word best expresses the relationship between the two sentences?
items.context_html: Parrotfish grind mouthfuls of coral skeleton with fused, beak-like teeth, digesting the algae and excreting the leftover minerals as fine white grains. <u>However,</u> a single large parrotfish can generate hundreds of pounds of sand in a year.
items.why_correct_md: The second sentence states the **effect** of the grinding described in the first, so a cause-and-effect transition is required.
items.why_tempted_md: The surprising statistic feels contrast-worthy, so 'However' seems to fit even though nothing is being opposed.
items.rule_md: 1) Read the sentence before and the sentence after the transition. 2) Label the relationship in your own words: opposes, illustrates, follows from, or happens alongside. 3) Match that label to the transition's job. 4) Reject any connector whose job doesn't match your label, no matter how smooth it sounds.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'However' signals contrast, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it (misconception: transition_wrong_logic_contrast).
per_choice_rationale.B: The sand production is the direct outcome of the grinding and excreting described first — a cause-and-effect link.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'For example' requires a general claim followed by an illustration; the first sentence makes no broad claim being illustrated (misconception: transition_false_example).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' marks two events unfolding at the same time in different places, not a causal chain (misconception: transition_time_for_logic).

hints.body_md: What relationship do you see between what the parrotfish does in the first sentence and what it produces in the second?
Transition words are logic labels. Decide first whether the second sentence opposes, illustrates, or follows from the first — then check your word against that logic.
The word you kept signals that the second sentence pushes back against the first. Is the sand production a surprise that contradicts the grinding, or a direct outcome of it?

Name the logic test: contrast words need opposing ideas. The second sentence gives the direct outcome of the grinding in the first, so a contrast word mislabels the link — pick the transition that announces cause and effect.
Before checking anything else, decide: is the second sentence giving one instance of a general claim, or telling you what the grinding leads to?
An illustration transition needs a general statement first and a specific case second. Test whether these two sentences fit that shape.
For your pick to fit, the first sentence would need to make a broad claim that the second illustrates with an example. Does the first sentence make such a claim?

Example transitions introduce a specific instance of a general statement, but this second sentence describes the outcome produced by the first sentence's action — cause and effect, not illustration. Re-label the logic and select again.
What would change if the two sentences were describing events happening side by side at the same time?
Time-based transitions and logic-based transitions do different jobs. Ask whether the sentences are linked by when they happen or by why the second one is true.
'Meanwhile' says two things are unfolding simultaneously in different places. Is that the connection between grinding coral and producing sand?

A simultaneity transition marks two separate events sharing a moment in time, but here the second sentence follows causally from the first — the grinding is what creates the sand. Choose the connector that signals an outcome.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to open the paragraph with a sentence that introduces its main focus. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: Each week, Rosa Alvarez interviews the family of every person who has died in Harper County, asking about nicknames, recipes, and small kindnesses. The finished obituaries often run longer than the front-page stories. Readers say they clip and save them, and some families frame them.

choices.label: Newspapers have printed obituaries for hundreds of years.
Rosa Alvarez has worked at the Ledger longer than any other employee.
Harper County has been losing population for decades.
At the Harper County Ledger, obituaries are treated as the paper's most careful journalism.

items.why_correct_md: It states the exact idea the details develop: this paper gives its obituaries **extraordinary care**, shown by the interviews, the length, and the readers who save them.
items.why_tempted_md: The tenure sentence tempts students because Rosa Alvarez stars in the paragraph's first body sentence.
items.rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences and state their shared subject in one phrase. 2) Ask what each opener promises the paragraph will discuss. 3) Eliminate openers broader or narrower than the shared subject. 4) Eliminate openers introducing facts the body never touches. 5) Keep the opener whose promise every body sentence helps keep.

per_choice_rationale.A: Too broad — it promises a history of obituaries in general, not this paper's distinctive practice.
per_choice_rationale.B: Wrong emphasis — it narrows the paragraph to one employee's tenure, which the details never discuss.
per_choice_rationale.C: Off-topic — population decline never appears anywhere in the paragraph.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: it names the paper and frames obituaries as its signature work, the idea every following sentence supports.

hints.body_md: Tell me what the rest of the paragraph covers, in one phrase — all newspapers ever, or one weekly's practice?
Openers set a scope. Compare the scope of your sentence to the scope of the details that follow it.
Your opener promises centuries of newspaper history. Which following sentence delivers on that promise?

An introduction must match the paragraph's actual scope; a claim about all newspapers over hundreds of years is far wider than these details about one weekly's obituary craft. Narrow the scope and re-choose.
What made you center the opener on one employee's length of service?
Test an opener by asking whether every later sentence develops it. Do the clipping, framing, and length details develop a tenure claim?
Does the paragraph ever mention how long anyone has worked there — or is it about how the obituaries themselves are produced and received?

A good opener predicts the paragraph's content; a tenure fact predicts a profile of one person's career, which never arrives. Your pick spotlights the employee instead of the work — re-aim at what the body sentences share.
Where does the paragraph ever return to the idea in your opener?
Check for orphan openers: an introduction that no body sentence follows up is off-focus no matter how true it is.
Population loss might explain why there are deaths to cover, but does any sentence here discuss the county shrinking?
Relevance rule: an opener must be developed by the sentences after it; a demographic trend the paragraph never mentions leaves the reader stranded. Drop the outside fact and re-choose.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to divide this paragraph into two paragraphs so that each one has a single focus. The most logical place to begin the new paragraph is at:
items.context_html: [1] The first darkrooms were portable tents that traveled by wagon alongside photographers of the 1850s. [2] Wet-plate negatives had to be developed within minutes, so the tent went wherever the camera did. [3] A modern darkroom, by contrast, is a fixed room built around running water and total control of light. [4] Its walls are painted a deep matte black, and its door is sealed with a folding light trap. [5] A ventilation fan pulls chemical fumes up and away from the printing bench.
items.why_correct_md: The topic **pivots** from historical tents to the modern room at the 'by contrast' sentence, so the new paragraph begins there.
items.why_tempted_md: Sentence 4's shift to physical details feels like a fresh start, but the modern-darkroom topic has already begun one sentence earlier.
items.rule_md: 1) Label each sentence's topic in two or three words. 2) Find where the labels change from one subject to another. 3) Start the new paragraph at the first sentence of the new subject. 4) Verify both resulting paragraphs read as single-focus units.

per_choice_rationale.A: Splits the tent history from its own explanation (divide_midtopic), since Sentence 2 still explains why the tents existed.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the paragraph pivots from 1850s tents to the modern room exactly at the 'by contrast' sentence.
per_choice_rationale.C: Breaks after the modern room has already been introduced (divide_late), stranding the topic sentence with the history.
per_choice_rationale.D: Leaves nearly all of the modern-room description in the first paragraph (divide_last_sentence), creating a one-sentence orphan.

hints.body_md: Walk me through the paragraph's two big topics — where does the first one actually end?
Check whether the wet-plate statement continues the tent story or starts something new before you split there.
'Negatives had to be developed within minutes' — is that still explaining the traveling tents of the 1850s?

A paragraph break belongs where the topic turns, and the second statement is still explaining why the old tents existed; splitting there orphans the history from its own explanation, so find the true pivot.
What made the painted-walls line feel like a fresh start to you?
Look one position earlier and ask whether the modern-darkroom topic has already begun by then.
If the new paragraph starts at the painted walls, which paragraph is left holding the line that announces the modern darkroom?

That line continues describing the modern room introduced just before it, so breaking there splits one topic down the middle; begin the new paragraph where the switch from past to present is first announced.
Tell me which topic the ventilation-fan line belongs with — the traveling tents or the fixed room?
Count how many statements describe the modern darkroom, then see how many your split would leave behind in the first paragraph.
Would a one-line second paragraph about a fan really carry a single focus equal to the rest?
Dividing at the final line leaves almost all of the modern-room description attached to the history; the break must fall where the paragraph first turns from past to present, so re-place it there.

items.stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?
items.context_html: The city promised new water spigots for the garden last spring. <u>Similarly,</u> the trenching work has been postponed twice.
items.why_correct_md: The delays **contradict** the expectation created by the promise, so the sentences need a contrast transition.
items.why_tempted_md: Both sentences concern the same spigot project, so students mistake shared topic for shared direction and keep the similarity word.
items.rule_md: 1) Restate each sentence in your own words. 2) Ask what the first sentence leads you to expect. 3) Decide whether the second sentence fulfills, reverses, causes, or illustrates that expectation. 4) Match the transition to that exact relationship. 5) Reread with the transition in place to confirm the logic.

per_choice_rationale.A: Wrong logic: a similarity transition claims the second sentence mirrors the first, but repeated delays cut against the promise.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the second sentence reverses the expectation set by the promise, which calls for a contrast transition.
per_choice_rationale.C: False cause: nothing about promising spigots produces the postponements.
per_choice_rationale.D: The delay is not an instance of the promise; it is evidence the promise is going unmet.

hints.body_md: What relationship did you see between the promise and the postponements?
Test the transition by restating each sentence in your own words and asking whether the second echoes the first or pushes against it.
Does a twice-delayed project resemble a promise being kept — and what does a similarity word claim about the two sentences?

A similarity transition tells readers the second sentence mirrors the first, but here the second sentence cuts against what was promised, so a likeness word misstates the logic — re-choose with the true relationship in mind.
How did you connect cause and effect between these two sentences?
Check the logic's direction: does the first sentence actually make the second one happen?
Would a promise of new spigots cause the digging to be postponed — or is the delay working against what was promised?

That transition asserts the first sentence produced the second, but nothing about the promise causes the delays; the second sentence undercuts the first instead — pick the connector that captures that tension.
In your own words, what would the second sentence be an example of?
Apply the illustration test: that kind of transition works only if sentence two is a specific instance of sentence one's claim.
Is a twice-postponed trench an instance of a promise being made, or evidence that the promise is not being kept?

An illustration transition requires the second sentence to exemplify the first, yet the delay contradicts the promise rather than illustrating it — reconsider which relationship the connector must express.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main point about what the letters reveal. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: For years, the letters my great-grandfather mailed from Buenos Aires sat in a shoebox labeled 'miscellaneous.' Last spring, my mother and I scanned all ninety-four of them and tagged each with its date and postmark. As we worked, we watched his Spanish creep into his Yiddish sentences, one borrowed word at a time.

choices.label: Scanning fragile letters requires patience and a steady flatbed scanner.
Read in order, the letters trace a man slowly turning into someone new.
Buenos Aires drew thousands of Eastern European immigrants into its port neighborhoods in the early twentieth century.
My mother hopes to read and digitize our photo albums next winter.

items.why_correct_md: It **restates the paragraph's discovery** — the gradual transformation visible across the letters — in a single closing image.
items.why_tempted_md: The historical statistic feels weighty and on-theme for immigration, but it widens the lens far beyond what these letters reveal.
items.rule_md: 1) Restate the paragraph's main point in your own words. 2) Ask what the stem requires the final sentence to do. 3) Test each option: does it return to that point, or drift to process, background, or future plans? 4) Eliminate any sentence introducing material the paragraph never developed. 5) Choose the one that echoes the main point.

per_choice_rationale.A: Ends on equipment and procedure, abandoning the paragraph's point about what the letters reveal.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: it restates the paragraph's discovery — a gradual transformation visible across the letters — in a closing image.
per_choice_rationale.C: Zooms out to a broad historical statistic, widening the lens far beyond this one family's papers.
per_choice_rationale.D: Pivots to a future project, introducing material the paragraph never developed.

hints.body_md: Think back to the stem — what main point is the closing sentence supposed to reinforce?
Separate the paragraph's subject (what the letters show) from its method (how you handled them), and check which one your sentence extends.
Does equipment advice tell us anything about what the writing in those envelopes revealed?

A concluding sentence must return to the paragraph's central discovery — the change visible across the correspondence — not to the mechanics of scanning; this pick ends on procedure. Re-choose the sentence that echoes the discovery.
If you covered up the rest of the passage, would this closer sound like it belongs to one family's story or to a textbook?
Match the scope of the final sentence to the scope of the paragraph — one family's papers versus a whole migration wave.
Does a continent-wide statistic reinforce what these particular pages showed about one person?

The paragraph is intimate and specific, so a broad demographic claim widens the lens instead of reinforcing the point about what the pages reveal; the conclusion must stay with this one writer's gradual shift. Re-choose with that focus.
What made a sentence about future projects feel like a wrap-up for this paragraph?
Check the timeline: a conclusion should look back over what this paragraph established, not ahead to a different task.
Do photo albums and next winter's plans reinforce what the ninety-four pages already revealed?

Ending on an upcoming project introduces unrelated material rather than reinforcing the paragraph's point about what the correspondence shows; a strong closer circles back to that revelation. Re-choose the sentence that does so.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to add the following sentence: "A porter's shifts could stretch to four hundred hours a month, with only brief naps snatched between stations." To preserve the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, where should the sentence be placed?
items.context_html: [1] The Pullman Company hired formerly enslaved men as sleeping-car porters soon after the Civil War. [2] Porters greeted passengers, converted seats into berths, and answered call bells at every hour of the night. [3] Despite that grueling load, the job offered steady wages and a rare chance to travel. [4] In 1925, porters organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, which became the first Black-led union to win a contract with a major American corporation.
items.why_correct_md: The sentence supplies the workload that Sentence 3's phrase 'that grueling load' points **back** to.
items.why_tempted_md: Placing it after Sentence 3 tempts readers because both discuss hardship, but the pointer phrase must follow its evidence, not precede it.
items.rule_md: 1) Find pointer words in the paragraph ('that,' 'this,' 'despite'). 2) Ask what each pointer refers to. 3) Place the new sentence so every pointer still has its referent behind it. 4) Reread the paragraph start to finish to confirm the flow.

per_choice_rationale.A: Opening with shift lengths would dangle a detail before readers even know who porters were.
per_choice_rationale.B: Correct: the hours extend the list of duties in Sentence 2 and set up 'that grueling load' in Sentence 3.
per_choice_rationale.C: After Sentence 3, the detail trails the phrase that summarizes it, weakening the 'despite' contrast.
per_choice_rationale.D: Tacked on after the union milestone, the sentence yanks readers back in time and buries the paragraph's climax.

hints.body_md: What would a first-time reader need to know before hearing about four-hundred-hour months?
Check what the proposed sentence assumes the reader already understands — job titles need prior introductions.
If the paragraph opened with this workload detail, who would 'a porter' be to a reader who hasn't met the Pullman Company yet?

New sentences must follow the information they depend on; this one presumes porters have been introduced and their duties sketched, so it cannot lead the paragraph. Trace where its supporting context ends and place it there.
Which earlier phrase does the expression 'that grueling load' point to?
Pointer phrases like 'that' must look backward at something already stated — check what Sentence 3 can see behind it from each position.
If the hours detail arrives only later, what exactly was 'that grueling load' referring to when readers first hit it?

A summarizing pointer works only when its evidence comes first; parking the workload detail behind the contrast sentence leaves the pointer starved and the detail stranded. Re-place the sentence so the pointer has its referent.
Where does the paragraph's story reach its destination, and what happens if new hardship details come after that?
Watch the chronology: the paragraph moves from hiring to duties to a 1925 milestone — test each slot against that arc.
Once the union's victory closes the story, does circling back to monthly hours push the paragraph forward or drag it backward?

Supporting details belong before the conclusion they justify; adding workload facts after the climactic milestone breaks the timeline and blunts the ending, so slot the sentence where it feeds the hardship discussion.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph with a sentence that reinforces its main idea about the resourcefulness of sound-effects technicians. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: Live radio drama depended on improvised sound effects. A sheet of cellophane, crumpled near the microphone, became a crackling campfire; coconut shells clopped like horses on cobblestones; a knife driven into a cabbage stood in for grim business offstage. Technicians rehearsed these tricks as carefully as the actors rehearsed their lines.

choices.label: Radio dramas eventually gave way to television in the 1950s.
Many radio actors later found steady work in film and television.
With nothing but everyday odds and ends, these artists could conjure a storm, a stampede, or a murder.
Cellophane, patented years earlier, had dozens of uses outside the studio.

items.why_correct_md: A strong conclusion **circles back** to the paragraph's governing idea — here, the technicians' inventiveness with humble props — and generalizes it.
items.why_tempted_md: The historical note about television feels like a natural 'ending' because it closes the era, but it abandons the paragraph's actual subject.
items.rule_md: 1) State the paragraph's main idea in one clause. 2) Check each option: does it restate or extend that idea, or introduce a new subject? 3) Eliminate options about different people, later eras, or single details. 4) Pick the sentence that widens the examples back into the main idea. 5) Reread the paragraph with it in place.

per_choice_rationale.A: Pivots to the medium's later decline, abandoning the paragraph's subject of ingenious effects work.
per_choice_rationale.B: Spotlights the actors' future careers instead of the technicians the paragraph has been praising.
per_choice_rationale.C: Correct: it gathers the paragraph's examples into a closing statement about what the technicians could create from humble materials.
per_choice_rationale.D: Burrows into trivia about one prop rather than widening back to the technicians' inventiveness.

hints.body_md: What's the writer trying to leave the reader with, according to the stem?
Match your closing sentence against the paragraph's actual subject — who is it about, and what quality of theirs?
Does a note about the medium's later decline reinforce what the crew could do with household props, or change the subject to broadcast history?

A concluding sentence must circle back to the paragraph's main idea — the crew's ingenuity with humble props — and this one pivots to the fate of the whole medium instead; re-choose the sentence that stays on that idea.
Which people does the paragraph spend its energy on?
Check the cast of characters: a strong conclusion should spotlight the same group the paragraph has been praising.
The paragraph's examples are all about effects work behind the microphone — does a sentence about the performers' later careers reinforce that?

This closer trades the paragraph's real subject, the effects crew, for the actors' future employment, so it cannot reinforce the stated main idea; re-choose the sentence that keeps the crew and their improvised craft in view.
If you covered up the stem's stated goal, would this sentence still read like a summary or like a side note?
Watch for the trivia trap: a fact about one prop is narrower than the paragraph's governing idea.
Does the history of cellophane speak to the crew's inventiveness, or only to one material they happened to use?
A conclusion should widen back to the paragraph's central claim rather than burrow into a single prop's backstory; this sentence does the latter, so re-choose the one that celebrates the whole craft.

items.stem_md: The writer wants to add a sentence at the beginning of the paragraph that introduces its main idea. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
items.context_html: Writing ink of the fifteenth century was water-based and flowed easily from a quill, but it beaded and smeared on metal type. Gutenberg's workshop instead blended lampblack with linseed varnish, producing a paste sticky enough to cling to each letter. The mixture transferred cleanly under pressure and dried to a durable sheen.

choices.label: Ink has been made from countless materials over the centuries.
Lampblack is a fine soot gathered from burning oil or resin.
Printing from metal type demanded an ink unlike any a scribe had ever used.
Gutenberg borrowed the screw mechanism of his press from local wine makers.

items.why_correct_md: The best introduction previews the paragraph's **controlling idea**, which each later sentence then develops.
items.why_tempted_md: The broad ink-history opener attracts students who equate 'introduction' with 'general background.'
items.rule_md: 1) Read the body sentences first and summarize their shared subject in one phrase. 2) Ask of each candidate: does it promise exactly that subject? 3) Reject candidates that are wider, narrower, or about something else. 4) Confirm the survivor lets the next sentence follow naturally. 5) Re-read the assembled paragraph from the top.

per_choice_rationale.A: This sentence is far broader than the paragraph, which concerns one specific formulation problem.
per_choice_rationale.B: This zooms in on a single ingredient before the paragraph has established why a new recipe was needed.
per_choice_rationale.C: This states the paragraph's controlling idea — a new craft required an entirely new ink — which every following sentence supports.
per_choice_rationale.D: The press's mechanics are a different subject; the paragraph never discusses machinery.

hints.body_md: If you covered up the candidates, how would you summarize what this paragraph is actually about?
Match the opener's scope against the paragraph's scope — a good first line promises neither more nor less than what follows.
Would a reader promised a sweep of centuries and countless materials be satisfied by three sentences about one workshop's recipe?
An opener spanning all of ink history promises far more than this tightly focused paragraph delivers; the first line must fit the paragraph's actual scope. Re-test each candidate against the body.
What job should the very first sentence of a paragraph perform for a reader?
Check the order of information: details usually earn their place only after the main point stands.
Can a reader make sense of one ingredient's origin before learning why a fresh recipe mattered at all?
Leading with a single ingredient buries the paragraph's larger point beneath a supporting detail; an introduction must frame the whole before the parts. Reconsider which candidate frames it.
Tell me what convinced you the press machinery belongs at the top of this paragraph.
Trace each body sentence and ask whether the proposed opener's subject appears again anywhere.
If the following sentences never mention screws or machinery, what happens to the promise that opener makes?

An introduction must announce the subject the paragraph develops, and nothing after this candidate returns to press hardware — the opener would point readers down the wrong path. Match the opener to the body's true subject.

items.stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition between the two sentences?
items.context_html: Requeening usually calms an aggressive colony. <u>Even so,</u> the hive's temperament may take six weeks to soften, because the old queen's defensive daughters must live out their lifespans first.
items.why_correct_md: The second sentence attaches a **concession** — the fix works, but slowly — so a yes-but transition fits the logic.
items.why_tempted_md: Because requeening does eventually calm the hive, students read the delay as a consequence of the fix and pick 'Consequently.'
items.rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one's claim. 2) Ask what sentence two does to that claim: extends it, restates it, illustrates it, or qualifies it. 3) If sentence two admits a complication while leaving the claim standing, choose a concessive transition. 4) Confirm by reading the pair with a plain 'but still' in the slot — if that works, the concession reading is right.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the second sentence concedes a lingering complication that qualifies the calming claim, exactly the yes-but relationship 'Even so' signals.
per_choice_rationale.B: 'Consequently' would present the six-week delay as flowing naturally from the calming claim, but the delay tempers that claim rather than resulting from it.
per_choice_rationale.C: 'In other words' signals a paraphrase, yet the second sentence adds new, qualifying information instead of restating the first.
per_choice_rationale.D: 'For instance' would require the delay to be an example of requeening's calming effect, but it is a caveat working against that effect.

hints.body_md: What made the second sentence feel like a direct outcome of the first?
This is a transition-logic check: ask whether sentence two extends the first claim or qualifies it.
Requeening calms the hive — but the temperament takes six weeks to soften. Is that delay a consequence of the calming, or a catch attached to it?

A cause-and-effect connector would present the slow softening as flowing naturally from the calming claim, but the sentence actually tempers that claim with a lingering complication; the passage needs a concession, not a consequence. Reconsider with that relationship in mind.
In your reading, how does sentence two restate sentence one?
Apply the restatement test: a rephrasing transition works only if both sentences say the same thing differently.
Does 'temperament takes six weeks to soften' repeat 'requeening calms the colony' in new words, or add a limitation to it?

A paraphrase signal requires the second sentence to restate the first, yet this sentence introduces new, qualifying information about a delay; a concessive connector fits the logic. Re-test the options against both sentences.
Which general claim did you see the six-week delay exemplifying?
Check the illustration relationship: sentence two must be a specific instance of sentence one for that connector to hold.
Is a six-week lag one example of requeening calming a hive — or a caveat that pushes against the calming claim?

An example connector needs sentence two to give a case of sentence one, but the delay is a qualification, not an example; the logic calls for a yes-but move. Re-read the pair and match the connector to that move.

items.stem_md: Which choice provides the most logical transition from the preceding sentence?
items.context_html: Peregrine falcons treat high-rise ledges much as their ancestors treated sea cliffs. <u>Indeed,</u> several downtown pairs now fledge more chicks each season than pairs nesting on natural rock.
items.why_correct_md: The second sentence **confirms and amplifies** the first with evidence, which is precisely the relationship 'Indeed' announces.
items.why_tempted_md: Because the second sentence compares city pairs with cliff pairs, many students misread the comparison as a contrast and reach for an opposition word.
items.rule_md: 1) Summarize sentence one's claim in your own words. 2) Ask what sentence two does to that claim: oppose it, result from it, illustrate it, or intensify it. 3) Match the transition to that exact function. 4) Beware of surface comparisons that are actually support. 5) Re-read the pair with your transition to confirm the logic holds.

per_choice_rationale.A: Correct: the second sentence intensifies and confirms the first claim with striking evidence, exactly the job of 'Indeed.'
per_choice_rationale.B: 'In contrast' asserts opposition, but the chick data supports rather than opposes the ledges-as-cliffs claim (transition_false_contrast).
per_choice_rationale.C: 'Otherwise' sets up a what-if alternative, yet the second sentence describes what actually happens (transition_false_condition).
per_choice_rationale.D: 'Meanwhile' juxtaposes simultaneous scenes, but these sentences form a claim followed by its supporting evidence (transition_false_time).

hints.body_md: What claim does the first sentence make, stated in your own words?
Decide whether the second sentence opposes the first or pushes the same point even further before you label the logic.
Fledging more chicks downtown than on rock faces — does that undercut the ledges-as-cliffs comparison, or confirm it emphatically?
The second sentence intensifies the first rather than opposing it, so a contrast connector reverses the passage's logic. Choose the connector that strengthens the claim instead of contradicting it.
What would change if the first sentence turned out to be false?
This connector family implies 'if not for that.' Test whether the second sentence describes what happens in the absence of the first.
Does the chick data describe what occurs if falcons did not treat ledges like cliffs — or what happens precisely when they do?
'Otherwise' signals an alternative scenario, but the second sentence is direct evidence for the first claim, not a what-if. Re-select the connector that presents confirming evidence.
Where does time actually matter in these two sentences?
Check whether the sentences describe two simultaneous scenes or one claim followed by its support.
Is the passage cutting between two things happening at once, or driving deeper into a single point about falcon success?
'Meanwhile' juxtaposes parallel events, yet these sentences form claim-plus-evidence; the connector should affirm and amplify. Re-examine the options with that relationship in mind.

items.stem_md: Which transition word best expresses the relationship between these two sentences?
items.context_html: For three weeks, every instrument pointed to an eruption from the summit crater, and the observatory said so publicly. <u>Therefore,</u> the outbreak, when it finally came, tore open a fissure far down the volcano's northern flank.
items.why_correct_md: The eruption **defied** the forecast, so the transition must concede that the expected outcome failed to occur.
items.why_tempted_md: The first sentence builds a strong forecast, so a conclusion word feels like the natural payoff — until you notice the eruption happened in the wrong place.
items.rule_md: 1) Ask what the first sentence leads the reader to expect. 2) Ask whether the second sentence fulfills or breaks that expectation. 3) Fulfilled → result word; broken → concession word; restated → clarification word. 4) Insert your choice and re-read for logic.

per_choice_rationale.A: 'Therefore' treats the flank eruption as the predicted outcome, but the eruption defied the summit forecast.
per_choice_rationale.B: The actual outbreak is not similar to the forecast; it departs from it.
per_choice_rationale.C: The second sentence does not restate the forecast in different words — it contradicts it.
per_choice_rationale.D: Correct: despite the confident forecast, the eruption broke the expectation, which calls for a concession.

hints.body_md: Before checking the connector, what did the instruments lead everyone to expect — and what actually happened?
A conclusion word claims the second sentence follows naturally from the first. Verify that the outcome matches the prediction.
The forecast named the summit; the fissure opened far down the flank. Is that the predicted result, or a surprise that broke the prediction?
A result transition only fits when expectation and outcome line up; here the eruption defied the forecast, so the sentence needs a concession word instead. Re-choose with that reversal in mind.
